analysis.one_liner: Bans debt collectors from trying to collect debts that are too old to sue over.
analysis.headline: The bill would bar debt collectors from pursuing debts whose legal time limit has expired; it has no cosponsors and has sat in the House Financial Services Committee since April 2025 with no action.
analysis.plain_summary: When a debt is past its statute of limitations — usually three to ten years, depending on the state and the type of debt — the creditor can no longer win a lawsuit over it, but collectors can still call, write, and demand payment, and a partial payment can restart the clock. H.R. 2704 would amend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to make it a federal violation for a debt collector to collect or attempt to collect any debt whose time limit has expired. Rep. Steve Cohen introduced it on April 8, 2025, and it was sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has not moved since. No other member has cosponsored it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers being pursued over old, legally expired debts. These are often people who fell behind years ago and have since moved on; they get calls and letters demanding payment on a debt a court would no longer enforce, and many pay or make a small payment — which can restart the clock — without knowing their rights. The bill would make those collection attempts a federal violation under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers hounded over old expired debts

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a violation of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act for a collector to collect or attempt to collect any debt once the statute of limitations has expired, taking away the main leverage behind threats to restart the clock on old debt.
Because the ban is written into a federal consumer protection law, it applies nationwide, protecting consumers in every state rather than only those whose state law already restricts the practice.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collectors and debt buyers, who profit from purchasing old charged-off debt cheaply and pressing people to pay on accounts that are past the legal time limit. If the bill passed, that portion of their business would be off the table. Consumers who still feel morally bound to pay an old debt could still do so voluntarily; the bill only bars collectors from pursuing or attempting to collect such debts.

drawbacks.text: The bill is extremely narrow: it adds one sentence to the existing debt collection law and does not address related problems such as creditors suing consumers on time-barred debts or suing before a consumer can raise the expired deadline in court.

Debt collectors would lose the ability to pursue old debts, which the industry argues can still be legitimate obligations; collectors and debt buyers who rely on older portfolios would see some accounts become uncollectible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is real but targeted: it would end a practice that mostly traps people who are already financially stressed and often without a lawyer. The cost to collectors is modest — they would lose access to a slice of debt that is legally stale, and the industry has operated under similar restrictions in several states without collapsing. The bill is one sentence long and does not address related gaps, such as lawsuits filed on stale debts before the debtor can raise the expired deadline as a defense, so a fair criticism is that it is narrow. But its aim is straightforward and its drawback is limited scope, not a serious cost to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action; with no cosponsors, nothing is moving it forward.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Fair Debt Collection Improvement Act on April 8, 2025, to amend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.
The bill would add a new provision stating that a debt collector may not collect, or attempt to collect, any consumer debt whose governing statute of limitations has expired.
The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee the same day, and no further action has been taken since.
No other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: debt collectors can still pursue time-barred debts, which is worth money to collection firms and debt buyers, while consumers remain exposed to demands on old debt. The bill is not dead — the current Congress runs into early 2027 — but nothing is moving it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors and debt buyers, for now

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 8, 2025; it was his action alone that put the proposal before the House.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member has acted on the bill — its Democratic sponsor — and it has no cosponsors from either party, so no party split has taken shape.

industries.industry: Debt collection and debt buying industry
industries.note: The bill would make it a federal violation to collect or attempt to collect any debt past its statute of limitations, cutting off a portion of the aged debt these firms buy and pursue. For consumers, this removes the tactic of threatening old debt to trick someone into restarting the clock on it, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Creditors and lenders who sell or assign charged-off debt
industries.note: Banks, credit card issuers, and other lenders that sell charged-off accounts to buyers would find some of those old accounts worth less, since a buyer could no longer legally pursue debts past their legal time limit.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the House Financial Services Committee for months with no cosponsors and no hearing. A first-term solo bill with zero cosponsors rarely advances; unless the sponsor attracts support or the committee takes an interest, it will most likely remain without action until the Congress ends in January 2027.
